item.title: Thousands run Cuba’s Marabana marathon as many protest US sanctions
item.description:
Thousands run Cuba’s Marabana marathon as many protest US sanctions
Thousands of people have run in Cuba’s Marabana marathon, using the event to protest U.S. economic sanctionsByANDREA RODRIGUEZ Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 10:56 AM
Share
HAVANA -- Thousands of people ran Sunday in Cuba’s most important international marathon, with some using the race to protest U.S. economic sanctions against the island.
The Marabana marathon, held every November to commemorate the founding of Havana, took runners along city's iconic streets and landmarks, such as the Paseo del Prado and the Capitol building. Many wore signs expressing solidarity with Cuba.
“Cuba is not a threat; the blockade is,” read the signs that many of the 3,000 participants wore on their backs.
The U.S. embargo against Cuba was first imposed in 1960, after Fidel Castro led a revolution that toppled dictator Fulgencio Batista and nationalized properties belonging to U.S. citizens and corporations. As a result, the Caribbean country has endured decades of economic and financial troubles and is now being pushed to a breaking point after U.S. President Donald Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba.
The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that disrupt water supplies and internet and telephone services.
“The blockade is suffocating the Cuban people," Yuraldi Cava, a 58-year-old state employee, said while running. “We are going to win this fight.”
Mayté Vigoa, Havana’s provincial government coordinator for sports, said the city had to make a major effort to hold the international race because of the island’s precarious economic conditions. She confirmed that the sportswear brand Adidas, a longtime sponsor of the competition, did not provide support this year.

item.title: Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
item.description:
Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against a government plan to overhaul funding for public broadcastersByKAREL JANICEK ASSOCIATION PRESS Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 10:22 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
PRAGUE -- Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy.
The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country.
The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy.
“We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said.
Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations.
Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
“We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another.

item.title: Zelenskyy warns Starshield restrictions threaten Ukraine’s energy defenses
item.description:
Zelenskyy warns Starshield restrictions threaten Ukraine’s energy defenses
Restrictions on the system hamper Kyiv’s ability to shoot down Russian drones.BySAMYA KULLAB Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 9:04 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
KYIV, Ukraine -- Restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield satellite communications system are hindering its ability to intercept Russian drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.
He warned that limitations on the system, operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, could weaken defenses around Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the winter months, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted the power grid.
Ukraine’s interceptor drones continue to lose contact with their operators when flying faster than 161 kph (100 mph) along the front line and over Russian-occupied territory, leaving them unable to catch Russian Shahed drones, Zelenskyy said.
“We are counting on these restrictions to be lifted,” he wrote on social media. “The protection of lives and Ukrainian energy infrastructure before winter depends on this. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defense, and the President’s Office have been instructed to work closely with the American side and SpaceX. It is important to be on the right side of history. We need to help Ukraine.”
Zelenskyy questioned Saturday whether the problem was technical, saying the restrictions appeared to have been imposed by SpaceX despite earlier assurances from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Starshield was more under U.S. government control.
Meanwhile, a Russian strike on Chornomorsk, a port city in Ukraine’s Odesa region, injured six people and damaged energy infrastructure, regional head Oleh Kiper said Sunday on Telegram.
The blast and falling debris also damaged a gas pipeline and nearby residential buildings, while two parked cars caught fire.

item.title: Southeast Asian leaders denounce violence in Myanmar and extend ban on its leader
item.description:
Southeast Asian leaders denounce violence in Myanmar and extend ban on its leader
Southeast Asian leaders say Myanmar has failed to comply with a 2021 peace plan and its military and armed groups continue to attack civiliansByJIM GOMEZ Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 8:18 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
MANILA, Philippines -- Southeast Asian leaders said Sunday that Myanmar has failed to comply with a 2021 peace plan and that its military and other armed groups continue to attack civilians, prompting them to extend a ban on Myanmar's leader attending the bloc's annual summits.
The stern rebuke by leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, who opened their annual summit meetings in the Philippine capital on Sunday, came during a review of the progress on the five-point peace plan by the country's military-backed government. Myanmar is a member of the 11-nation regional bloc.
ASEAN leaders proposed the plan in April 2021 to try to ease the violence that erupted after the army seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi. The army’s takeover triggered widespread pro-democracy protests that were brutally quashed, leading to armed resistance and a civil war that has spread over much of the country.
The leaders reiterated “deep concern” over insufficient progress in implementing the peace plan. They urged all parties and stakeholders in Myanmar, "in particular the armed forces, security forces and armed groups to de-escalate violence and stop targeted attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure and enhance trust-building efforts.”
Last month, a United Nations rights investigator said the military-backed government in Myanmar was intentionally attacking civilians to terrorize them and force them into submission.

item.title: Pope crosses Peru in finale of trip home to visit flock high in Andes, deep in Amazon
item.description:
Pope crosses Peru in finale of trip home to visit flock high in Andes, deep in Amazon
The plight of Indigenous peoples and the protection of the Amazon take center stage on Pope Leo XIV’s penultimate day in Peru as he visits communities in the Andes and the rainforestByMAURICIO SAVARESE Associated Press, NICOLE WINFIELD Associated Press, and ASTRID SUAREZ Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 6:53 AM
CUSCO, Peru -- The plight of Indigenous peoples and the protection of the Amazon take center stage Sunday as Pope Leo XIV travels across Peru to visit communities high in the Andes and deep in the rainforest.
On the penultimate day of his visit to his adopted homeland, Leo is expected to echo Pope Francis, emphasizing Catholic teaching that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.
He travels first to Cusco, the former capital of the Inca empire, before flying to the Amazonian city of Pucallpa, where illegal mining, deforestation and threats to Indigenous communities will be central concerns.
“The church in Peru perceives the continuity of his commitment to accompany Indigenous peoples in the defense of life and the care of the territory, which is increasingly threatened by deforestation and illegal mining,” Peruvian Cardinal Pedro Barreto, president of the Amazon bishops conference, told The Associated Press.
“Leo is clearing the path laid out” by Francis on environmental protection and human rights, Barreto said. He added that the pope would hear about violence affecting children and young people.
The visit to Cusco, 3,400 meters (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, will test the stamina of the pope, who is recovering from lung cancer surgery.
His schedule begins at the historic Sacsayhuamán fortress, where he will speak about local religious devotion. item.title: Spain says nearly 2,200 migrants reached Canary Islands in 2 days
item.description:
Spain says nearly 2,200 migrants reached Canary Islands in 2 days
Spain's maritime rescue service says nearly 2,200 migrants have arrived in the Canary Islands over the past two daysByThe Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 6:18 AM
MADRID -- Nearly 2,200 migrants have arrived by boat in Spain’s Canary Islands over the past two days, Spain’s maritime rescue service said Sunday.
The Spanish archipelago off northwest Africa is one of the main entry points for migrants into the country, as people mainly from West Africa attempt the dangerous Atlantic crossing in ramshackle boats. Of the just over 28,000 people who arrived in Spain by sea between January and the end of October, more than 13,000 arrived in the Canary Islands, according to the Interior Ministry.
The Maritime Rescue Service said it had assisted 1,324 migrants aboard 14 dinghies, most of whom arrived on the island of El Hierro. The figure was close to the daily record for this route — 1,461 people rescued on Nov. 7, 2020.
The strip of the Atlantic Ocean between West Africa and the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration routes. The islands are roughly 65 miles (105 kilometers) from the closest point in Africa, but to avoid security forces, many migrants attempt longer journeys that can take days or weeks. The majority depart from Mauritania.

item.title: Cape Verde could elect first woman president since gaining independence in 1975
item.description:
Cape Verde could elect first woman president since gaining independence in 1975
Cape Verde could elect its first woman president as former Justice Minister Joana Rosa challenges incumbent José Maria NevesByThe Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 12:22 AM
Cape Verde could elect its first woman president Sunday as former Justice Minister Joana Rosa challenges incumbent José Maria Neves, who is seeking a second term.
Six candidates are competing, with a runoff scheduled for Nov. 29 if no candidate receives more than half the votes.
Rosa, backed by the opposition Movement for Democracy, is the first woman to run for president since independence from Portugal in 1975. Women have held senior cabinet posts, but Cape Verde has never had a female prime minister or president.
In Cape Verde’s parliamentary system, the prime minister directs government policy and holds most executive authority. The president’s role is largely symbolic, although the directly elected head of state can veto legislation.
The Atlantic island nation off West Africa, home to about half a million people, has a record of peaceful transfers of power and competitive elections in a region where that is rare. Nearly 77,000 Cape Verdeans abroad are registered to vote, almost a fifth of the total electorate.
Many voters feel distant from their leaders and want a president who understands their daily difficulties, while limited economic prospects were driving young people to seek opportunities abroad, said Roselma Évora, a professor of political science and gender studies at the University of Cabo Verde.
Neves, who won in 2021 with about 52% of the vote, has pledged to build cross-party support to improve housing, healthcare and education, create jobs and raise wages.
Incumbency gives Neves greater visibility, including among overseas voters, Évora said.

item.title: Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda
item.description:
Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda
Southeast Asian leaders have opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila for three days of talksByJIM GOMEZ Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 12:13 AM
Share
MANILA, Philippines -- Southeast Asian leaders opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila on Sunday for three days of talks, including dialogues with world leaders led by U.S. President Donald Trump, whose crucial trip to Asia could help boost his standing after his party’s defeat in the midterm elections.
The talks by the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their expanded discussions with Asian and Western heads of state would focus on the world’s most troubling conflicts led by the war in the Middle East, according to drafts of post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press.
Trump is expected to land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. turns over the regional bloc’s rotating annual leadership to Singapore, Philippine officials said.
The ASEAN leaders are likely to renew calls for self-restraint and peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including longstanding disputes in the South China Sea and a civil war in Myanmar. They also are expected to press efforts to shield their economies and citizens from continuing fallout from intractable global conflicts.
“We reaffirmed our shared commitment to upholding international law, including the United Nations Charter,” the leaders’ draft statement says.
The statement also underlines the “importance of the peaceful resolution of disputes, upholding freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the sea, including the right of transit passage in straits used for international navigation.”

item.title: Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo 6 months into response
item.description:
Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo 6 months into response
Congo’s Ebola outbreak remains out of control six months after it was announced, with more than 11,000 cases recorded and nearly half proving fatalByThe Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 12:02 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BUNIA, Congo -- Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering.
More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.
Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities’ ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year.
By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country’s 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire.
New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained health care system.
Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities.
One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission.
Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over pay that is months overdue, sometimes leaving patients with confirmed infections without treatment.

item.title: Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them
item.description:
Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them
Millions of Argentines have turned out to see Pope Leo XIV — and the words that moved them most often belonged to his predecessor, and their compatriot, FrancisByISABEL DEBRE Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 12:00 AM
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- Vast crowds of young Argentines, a generation that Catholic leaders had feared was abandoning the pews, packed the parks of Buenos Aires and cheered as if at a concert when Pope Leo XIV promised a church open to “todos, todos, todos” — everyone, everyone, everyone.
Those words, like all of Leo’s surest applause lines during the visit, belonged to his Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis. So did much of the week's adulation.
Francis’ fierce defense of the downtrodden made him a moral voice abroad but long embroiled him in political fights at home — controversy that many believe deterred him from returning as pope. More than a year after his death, the more measured Leo made the homecoming Francis never could, carrying on his legacy and helping Argentines embrace their once-polarizing pope as a unifying national figure.
“It’s as though it has finally become clear that Francis left a very important legacy, not just for Argentina but for the universal church,” said Pablo Forni, a sociologist at Argentina’s national research council, Conicet. “Leo is reaping what Francis sowed.”
Billboards welcoming Leo bore Francis’ face. Pilgrims waved signs declaring “Francisco y León, un solo corazón” — Francis and Leo, one heart. Even libertarian President Javier Milei, who once insulted Francis as “the representative of evil on earth," declared Francis “the most important Argentine in history” at Leo's welcome ceremony, bringing a packed hall of his political allies and foes to its feet.
